Analysis of Winning Players in 20 Years of Professional Men’s Tennis Tournaments  
(ATP Grand Slams & Masters 1000 | 2001-2020)  
Identifying the performance metrics that best separate the top 8 winners of each tournament from the rest of field

By Kanak Somani

**Abstract**  
	This report aims to examine the key performance metrics that are the most consistent indicators of winning across elite men’s tournament matches. This analysis draws on match-level data across all Grand Slams and Masters 1000 tournaments from 2001-2020, which is then scoped down to top 8 player statistics vs the rest of the field. This project originated from an interest to analyze the factors behind the consistent winnings of the ‘Big Four’ tennis players during this time period. Essentially, what made these four players more likely to win, and win consistently, as opposed to the rest of the field. Although this project does not directly answer this original line of questioning, the purpose behind the project has remained the same \-  to analyze which factors contribute to winning.    
	  
**Question**  
 This report attempts to answer what performance metrics best distinguish winners over losers within high end men’s tennis tournaments. Although the original dataset contained all levels of tennis tournaments, only data from Grand Slams and Masters 1000s was chosen. This was mainly done due to the increased prevalence of higher quality players that are found in these tournaments. Furthermore, after this filter was completed, another filter was done to compare top 8 players to the rest of the tournament field. The reason top 8 players were chosen was primarily due to having a large enough sample size so that the data was not severely affected by any outliers. These findings are not to be used in a predictive manner; this is a descriptive, retrospective study only.   

**Data Sources and Methodology**  
The data source used was an ATP matches dataset that spanned 20 years of men’s tournaments results. This dataset spanned all levels of men’s tennis matches \- from amateur to grand slam. The dataset was organized on a per-match, per-tournament basis, where each match of a specific tournament took up 1 row. Once the appropriate filters were utilized, the next step was to establish the metrics to be analyzed. Some metrics were easily accessible, such as aces, break points faced and break points saved. Other metrics had to be computed, either explicitly due to the limitations of the dataset or implicitly using other available metrics. The information in the dataset was written in integer form, which contrasts with the usage of percentages in typical tennis analysis and statistics reports. After all the appropriate metrics were selected and calculated, the dataset was filtered for the winners of the round of 16\. This filter allowed for the comparison of the top 8 players of the selected tournaments versus the remainder of the field. The decision to select top 8 players, as opposed to any other rank, was because any fewer players would significantly amplify outliers and any more players would result in a muted analysis of the average. After filters and metrics were applied, results were first aggregated into a single row per tournament-year, as shown in Image 1\. However, this initial aggregation averaged each match's pre-computed percentage metrics directly — treating every match equally regardless of how many points or serves it actually contained. This produces a biased "average of averages" that doesn't match the true overall percentage across all matches combined. To correct this, a second aggregation was performed: the underlying raw counts (not the percentages) were summed first, and percentage-based metrics were then recalculated from those totals, as shown in Image 2

**Findings**  
**First serve percentage:**  
**Definition:** The percentage of serves that land within the box on the first attempt. One of the more commonly used statistics in tennis analysis \- used to signify serve accuracy.  
**Project Significance:** A comparative metric used to compare the top 8 players versus the rest of the field. A higher number is in favor of greater accuracy for the top 8 players.   
	  
The first metric examined was that of first serve percentage. First serve percentage is one of the most commonly cited statistics in all tennis analysis. The purpose of analyzing this statistic is to see if serve accuracy plays any role in advancing further into a tournament. As shown in image 3, there is very little difference in accuracy between top 8 players, in blue, and the rest of the field, in red.    
![First Serve Percentage by Surface Type](./Chart%20Images/1stSv%25.png)  
*Image 3*

Image 3 shows negligible difference in serve accuracy between top 8 players and the rest of the field and also between surfaces. All percentages, irrespective of surface, are above 60% accuracy, with the highest being approximately 65% on grass. Although first serve percentage remains a relevant statistic \- the more accurate your serve, the reduced likelihood of double faults \- it does not appear to be meaningful in determining a winner of any match. Because the difference in serve accuracy is negligible across both groups, it should not be treated as a meaningful differentiator when evaluating player quality or match outcome. 

**First Serve Win Percentage:**  
**Definition:** The percentage of first serves that landed inside the box, that were won by the server.  
**Project Significance:** A comparative metric between top 8 players versus the rest of the field. A higher number means top 8 players have a greater percentage of points won on their serves that have landed in, as opposed to the rest of the field. 

From first serve percentage, the natural extension is to analyze first serve win percentage. Any variation from accuracy to win percentage can provide a reason as to why certain players make it further in the tournament than others.   

![First Serve Win Percentage by Surface Type](./Chart%20Images/1stSvWin%25.png)  
*Image 4*   
	  
Image 4 shows that variation. Top 8 players are significantly more likely to win their first serves than the rest of the field, with the lowest win percentage still being 75%. Characteristics of grass courts, with their natural high speed and low bounce, explain the high percentage winning numbers. Characteristics of clay courts, with their natural low speed and high bounce, explain the relatively lower winning numbers. However, a different pattern emerges when examining the absolute difference between top 8 players and the rest of the field. In Image 5, the difference is marginally higher on clay courts. Taken together, the two images indicate that while top 8 players are more likely to win their first serves on grass courts, their performance advantage is far greater on clay courts. This perceived dominance on clay courts implies greater groundstroke placement of top 8 players, whereas the higher win percentages on grass courts implies greater serve quality of these same players.   
      
![First Serve Win Percentage delta by Surface Type](./Chart%20Images/1stSvWin%25_diff.png)  
*Image 5*

**First Serve Receive Win Percentage:**  
**Definition:** The percentage of serves that landed in that were won by the receiver. The inverse of the first serve win percentage metric  
**Project Significance:** First serves are typically faster and risk conducive as opposed to second serves. To be able to return first serves implies good defensive qualities, and a good baseline game. Comparative metric between top 8 players and the rest of the field. Higher numbers signify greater receiving ability. 

The return side of the game was also examined to determine whether a similar pattern holds. As shown in Image 6, top 8 players outperform the rest of the field by a wide margin. Most notably, the surface pattern runs in the opposite direction of the serve-side numbers in Image 4\. Return win percentage is highest on clay at around 38% and lowest on grass at around 31%. This inverse relationship is consistent with the natural characteristics of each surface type \- grass courts reward strong servers, so fewer points will be won on return. Clay courts have naturally slower serve speeds, and so a greater percentage of points won will be from rallies and returns. Combined with serve-side statistical findings, this supports the idea that top 8 players are better all-around players, winning more points regardless of service or returning.    
![1st Serve Return Win Percentage](./Chart%20Images/1stRtrWin%25.png)  
*Image 6*

**Second serve win percentage:**  
**Definition:** The percentage of second serves that landed in, that were won.  
**Project Significance:** Second serves are slower and more conservative, thereby making them easier to receive and enter into a rally. To win rallies consistently showcases groundstroke placement ability and also overall player quality. A comparative metric between top 8 players and rest of the field. Higher numbers show higher win percentage for the top 8 players.   
   
The next analysis centered on second serve win percentages. Unlike first serve win percentages which varied by surface, the surface variations are not as noticeable in second serve win percentages, as shown in Image 7\. Top 8 players win roughly 58%-60% of second serves, regardless of surface, while the rest of the field wins approximately 45%-47% of second serves. This consistency is the basis for establishing second serve win percentage as one of the key differentiators of winners over losers. Second serve does not bend to surface conditions the way first serves do, therefore making the surface-independence the best indicator of player quality. Furthermore, Image 8 supports the claim of player quality with a complementary metric. The difference percentage is markedly higher for each surface. For top 8 players to maintain a larger margin over the rest of the field even on slower, lower-risk serves indicates that player quality is more easily reflected in second serve performance. This surface-independence makes second serve win percentage a particularly reliable metric for establishing player quality across various tournament surfaces and conditions.              
![2nd Serve Win Percentage by Surface Type](./Chart%20Images/2ndSvWin%25.png)  
*Image 7*  
	  
![2nd Serve Win Percentage delta by Surface Type](./Chart%20Images/2ndSvWin%25_Diff.png)  
*Image 8*

**Break points faced/break points saved:**  
**Definition:**

1) Facing a break point, as a server, is when the receiver is one point away from winning a game. Break points can occur in the following situations: 0-40(3 break points), 15-40(2 break points), 30-40(1 break point), or 40-Adv.(1 break point)  
2) Saving a break point is when the server, facing a break point, wins the point instead. Saving a break point does not imply winning the game. It merely states that the server has won the point and thereby saved this particular break point.

**Project significance:** Break points are a crucial moment in tennis, both psychologically and momentum wise. Servers typically have a lot of power in tennis. Being able to decide where your serve lands and how fast you serve it gives you a greater chance at winning points. To have your serve “broken” is to give up that advantage and pass it over to your opponent. Break points faced is a share metric to quantify what percentage of total break points have been faced by the winner. A lower number is better. Break points saved is a delta metric between top 8 players and the rest of the field. The higher the number, the greater the chance to save a break point, which is usually in favor of the better player.   
   
The next piece of analysis centered on break points faced and saved. Break points are opportunities for the receiving side to win a game over the server. These are widely regarded as huge psychological breaks and momentum shifts within a match if converted. The theory was that top 8 players would face fewer break points and save a higher percentage of them, as mental fortitude is typically considered an important factor for making it far in any tournament. Image 9 supports the theory \- top 8 players faced fewer break points on average in a given match, and also won a higher percentage of the break points that they did face. The top 8 players face on average 5 break points per match and save on average 3, giving them a save rate of 60%. Meanwhile, the rest of the field faces 9 break points on average and saves on average 5 break points, giving them a save rate of 55%. Additional surface-level patterns include grass courts lagging noticeably in all sections of the graph \- most likely due to the prevalence of serve-side dominance. Clay court numbers are also higher, especially when looking at the rest of the field. As explained before, clay courts are typically slower and bounce higher and when a service is slow, especially second serves, that allows opportunities for rallies. This shows that avoiding pressure situations altogether is a stronger predictor of success, and a stronger indicator of overall player quality, than performance under pressure when it arises.       
![Break Points Faced and Break Points Saved](./Chart%20Images/bpFaced_bpSaved.png)  
*Image 9* 

**Aces:**  
**Definition:** An ace is a serve that is not hit/received, thereby qualifying it as a free point for the server.   
**Project Significance:** The stronger a player is at serves, the higher the percentage of hitting a serve. More aces hit in a match typically implies that the player is far better at service games than their opponent. Defined and analysed as a share metric: what percentage of total aces in a match belong to the winner.   
	The last metric to perform analysis on was aces. Aces are serves that go unreturned, effectively a free point for the server. The theory being tested was that players who advance further into a tournament are more likely to hit more aces per match than those who are eliminated early on. The ace analytics was performed as a share metric. As shown in Image 10, top 8 players, irrespective of surface, hit on average over half of all aces won. Grass courts show the highest ace share percentage due to conditions that favor servers, while clay courts show the lowest due to their conditions less favorable to servers. The lack of Wimbledon data in 2020 was due to the COVID-19  pandemic forcing the cancellation of the tournament. Because ace share is also sensitive to match length and format type (best of 3 versus best of 5), it should be treated as a supporting indicator rather than a true differentiator of player quality.     
![Ace Percentage Over Time by Surface Type](./Chart%20Images/ace%25.png)  
*Image 10*

**Conclusion:**  
This report examines the key performance metrics that are the most consistent indicators of winners versus losers across elite men’s tournament matches. This analysis draws on match-level and tournament-level data from all Grand Slams and Masters 1000 tournaments between 2001-2020, scoped down to the top 8 players vs the rest of the field. There are some findings that have stood out:

- First serve percentage has no impact on winners vs losers. At the elite level, winners and losers land their first serve at nearly identical rates.   
- Second serve win% is the single biggest factor in determining a winner from a loser. Unlike first serve statistics, second serves cannot be as easily manipulated by speed and accuracy, making it the cleanest indicator of overall player quality.   
- Return-side performance directly mirrors serve-side performances. This shows the top men’s players are not just specialists, they demonstrate strength across all aspects.   
- Ace% is a consistent differentiator, with top 8 players accounting for more than half of all aces across each tournament and surface. Aces are generally considered free points within the game of tennis. Winning approximately 55-60% of all aces in a match implies a gap of 10-20% more free points.  
- Break point avoidance has more weight than break point saves. Winners find themselves in pressure situations far less than the rest of the field do. While break point save rate does favor top 8 players, albeit marginally, it is the significant advantage in break point avoidance that truly differentiates winners over losers of any individual match.    
- Metrics are also surface dependent. Each surface has certain characteristics that lend themselves to certain playstyles. Faster surfaces tend to favor aggressive, service players whereas slower surfaces prefer defensive, baseline players.  
- Format length also plays a strong role in share-metrics. Formats that are best of 5, rather than best of 3, allow for inflated stats due to the increased length of the match. Increased length means more service points which then contribute to more opportunities for strong players to inflate statistics. Stats such as ace%, bpFaced% and bpSaved%\_difference are all affected by format length.
